What Ford did had nothing to do with a 'minimum wage'.

Ford paid his employees more to improve employee retention. When he introduced the production line, employee turnover was intense due to the repetitive boredom in what had previously been a highly skilled job. This resulted in a high costs to hire and train new (replacement) employees. The reality of this business decision was it was cheaper to pay the existing workers more to entice them to stay longer than to replace them.

Many businesses do this. A good example is Costco. They pay more than other retailers with a stated goal of maintaining a smaller, more stable workforce. It is worth noting that their business model (warehouse store) minimizes labor expense relative to other retailers. Instead of having people stock shelves, Costco parks pallets of merchandise on the floor.

For instance, while 'supply and demand' is simplistic, they embrace far more subtle and difficult concepts such as utility theory, i.e. it is the marginal utility of a thing that ultimately drives a decision to buy or not buy -- theory which is crucial to any discussion of price controls, which the minimum wage is.

The US constitution merely states natural born citizen.

As far as I know, the earliest known legal use of the term "natural born" stems from England where several statutes note:

British Foreign Protestants Naturalization Act 1708:

The children of all natural born subjects born out of the ligeance [i.e. out of England] of Her Majesty Her Heirs and Successors shall be deemed and adjudged to be natural born subjects of this Kingdom to all intents, constructions, and purposes whatsoever.

British Statute of 1730:

All Children born out of the Ligeance of the Crown of England, or of Great Britain, or which shall hereafter be born out of such Ligeance, whose Fathers were or shall be natural-born Subjects of the Crown of England, or of Great Britain, at the Time of the Birth of such Children respectively ... are hereby declared to be natural-born Subjects of the Crown of Great Britain, to all Intents, Constructions and Purposes whatsoever.

So there is some historical precedent that natural born citizens (subjects) are those born to current citizens (subjects) regardless of location. One could assume the framers of the constitution were familiar with this definition.

Ted Cruz (I believe) was born to 2 US citizens so by the above definitions would be considered a natural born citizen of the US.

To ensure birth within geographic boundaries the founding fathers should probably have used 'native born citizen' instead.

Wiki has a fairly in-depth analysis of it: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural-born-citizen_clause
